summary: Service oriented Laravel on AWS Elastic Beanstalk with Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL as the database; front end: React + Vite, Progressive Web App.

frontend.justification: Web: A client-rendered app behind login needs no server rendering. Fit for this project: strong performance, which you rated 5/5; well suited to gaming projects; strong time to market, which you rated 4/5. Mobile: Reuses the web app, installable without an app store. Fit for this project: strong time to market, which you rated 4/5; reuses the web codebase.

alternatives.why_not: Scored 0.7 points lower: the team would have to learn JavaScript/TypeScript; the chosen option wins on project.type (well suited to gaming projects).
Scored 0.8 points lower: the team would have to learn JavaScript/TypeScript; the chosen option wins on project.platforms (reuses the web codebase).

tradeoffs: Client-rendered: no SEO for public pages.
The team would have to learn JavaScript/TypeScript.
iOS limits background sync and push; browsers may evict offline storage.
Weaker camera/GPS/background-upload control than a native app.

backend.justification: Batteries-included PHP framework with queues and auth. Fit for this project: team.languages includes PHP; strong time to market, which you rated 4/5; built-in authentication; real-time needs an add-on (Channels).

alternatives.why_not: Scored 4.8 points lower: the team would have to learn C#; the chosen option wins on team.languages (team.languages includes PHP).
Scored 4.1 points lower: the team would have to learn JavaScript/TypeScript; proprietary API increases lock-in; the chosen option wins on team.languages (team.languages includes PHP).

tradeoffs: Long-lived WebSockets run in Laravel Reverb, a separate first-party process.
Per-request overhead is tight for p95=150ms.

database.choice: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL (us-east-1 N. Virginia)
database.justification: ACID transactions, JSONB, full-text search, PostGIS and pgvector in one engine. Fit for this project: strong performance, which you rated 5/5; strong time to market, which you rated 4/5.

alternatives.why_not: Scored 0.2 points lower: proprietary API increases lock-in; learning curve 4/5 for a intermediate team.

alternatives.choice: Amazon RDS for MySQL (us-east-1 N. Virginia)
alternatives.why_not: Scored 0.7 points lower: close runner-up; the chosen option combines better with the rest of the stack.

tradeoffs: Horizontal write scaling needs partitioning, read replicas or Citus.

hosting.justification: Managed web hosting on AWS (load balancer, auto scaling, health checks) without container orchestration. Fit for this project: strong time to market, which you rated 4/5; strong performance, which you rated 5/5.

alternatives.why_not: Scored 2.9 points lower: weaker overall fit once team skills, priorities and the other layers are combined.
Scored 3.3 points lower: weaker overall fit once team skills, priorities and the other layers are combined.

tradeoffs: Less flexible than ECS; platform versions must be kept current.

supporting.justification: Uses the backend framework's maintained auth library, so user data stays in your own database.
tradeoffs: Account recovery and MFA flows must still be designed.

supporting.choice: Nakama (open-source game server: matchmaking, realtime, leaderboards)
supporting.justification: Matches need an authoritative server that owns game state, matchmaking and per-room broadcast at low latency for 4000 concurrent players; leaderboards live in the database/Redis sorted sets.

alternatives.why_not: You would rebuild rooms, matchmaking and reconnection logic.
Managed and proven, but per-CCU pricing and vendor lock-in.

tradeoffs: Long-lived connections need sticky sessions or a pub/sub layer.

supporting.justification: Caches hot reads and sessions to hold p95=150ms, and doubles as the pub/sub and job-queue broker.

alternatives.why_not: No pub/sub or persistence, so it cannot double as a broker.
Every read hits the database at peak.

tradeoffs: Another stateful component to size and monitor.

supporting.justification: Moves slow or retry-prone work (background jobs) off the request path so p95 stays low and failures retry safely.

alternatives.why_not: Event-streaming platform: heavy to run for job queues at this scale.

tradeoffs: Jobs must be idempotent; monitor the dead-letter queue.

supporting.justification: Free push delivery to Android for messages that arrive while the app is closed.

alternatives.why_not: Costs per message and DLT templates.

tradeoffs: Notification payloads must not contain sensitive data.

supporting.justification: Runs tests and deploys on every merge; free minutes cover a small team.
Logs, metrics and traces stay in the same cloud and region as the data.

alternatives.why_not: Strong product but expensive per host at this budget.

assumptions: Scale level L3: ~80000 users, ~4000 peak concurrent, ~800 req/s at peak, ~156.2 GB stored
